title: What Quantitative Finance Is
objectives: Define quantitative finance as the application of mathematics, statistics and computing to pricing, risk, trading and investment problems
Identify the four main problem areas where quantitative methods are used in finance
Describe, at a high level, who works in quantitative finance and in what kinds of institutions
State what this platform does and does not promise, and how progress on it is measured
motivation: The phrase quant finance is used loosely in job advertisements, forums and films, which makes it genuinely hard to know what to learn, in what order, or whether you are making progress. This first lesson pins down a working definition, shows where the work happens and who does it, and sets out plainly what structured preparation can and cannot do for you, so that every later lesson on this platform has a purpose you can see.

blocks.md: **Quantitative finance** is the practice of applying mathematics, statistics and computing to problems of **pricing, risk, trading and investment**. It is not a separate science; it is a set of methods pointed at four concrete families of questions. *Pricing*: what is this contract worth today, an option, a bond, a complicated structured trade? *Risk*: how much can we lose, how likely is it, and what happens in bad scenarios? *Trading*: when and how should we buy or sell so that we transact efficiently and manage exposure in real time? *Investment*: how should a portfolio be constructed, and how do we know whether its performance came from skill or luck?

Each of those questions becomes a computation. A bank that promises a client a price for an option must compute that price from a model plus live market data, in seconds. A fund that holds thousands of positions must recompute its exposures overnight and answer: what happens to us if rates move 2 percent? A trading firm that quotes prices to the market must update quotes as order flow arrives, thousands of times per second. The common thread is that the answer is produced by a calculation, carried out by software, and someone's money depends on the calculation being right.

items: **Pricing and valuation**, models that turn market data into fair values for contracts.
**Risk management**, measuring exposures, stress-testing portfolios, computing regulatory capital.
**Trading and execution**, algorithms that quote, hedge and route orders.
**Investment and portfolio management**, signal research, allocation decisions, performance attribution.

blocks.md: Quantitative finance is not one employer or one job title; it is a method used across the whole industry. Investment banks such as JPMorgan and Goldman Sachs build pricing and risk systems for their trading desks and for regulatory reporting. Asset managers such as BlackRock use quantitative methods to manage index funds and to support active portfolio decisions at enormous scale. Hedge funds such as Two Sigma run research platforms whose whole purpose is turning data and statistics into trading decisions. Proprietary trading and market-making firms such as Jane Street, Citadel Securities and Optiver use mathematics and fast software to quote prices and manage risk continuously throughout the trading day. Around all of them sit exchanges, clearinghouses, data vendors such as Bloomberg, and regulators, all of which employ people who build and check quantitative systems. Later lessons in this module look at each institution type in detail.

The people doing the work fall into a few recognisable roles, quantitative researchers who design models, quantitative developers who turn models into reliable software, traders who make decisions with the models' help, and software engineers who build the surrounding platforms. The boundaries between these roles are real but blurry, and lesson 3 compares them directly.

blocks.title: What quantitative finance is not
blocks.md: It is not a scheme for guaranteed profits, models are approximations and markets punish overconfidence. It is not 'finance with some maths sprinkled on top': the mathematics is the substance, not decoration. And it is not only about trading screens, a great deal of the work is data engineering, numerical computing and careful software construction.

blocks.text: The platform's promise, and what it deliberately does not promise

blocks.md: This platform prepares you for quantitative finance honestly and measurably. *Honestly* means: the curriculum states its difficulty up front, teaches mathematics from zero rather than assuming it, goes deep into C++ because that is where much of the industry's critical software lives, and uses real finance rather than toy examples. *Measurably* means: every lesson has quizzes you can pass or fail, assessments that score specific skill areas, and projects with explicit evaluation criteria, your progress is a number you can check, not a feeling.

What the platform does **not** promise is equally important. It does not promise you a job, an interview, or any level of compensation; employment outcomes depend on hiring markets, timing, location and individual effort, and any course that guarantees them is telling you something untrue. What preparation can do, and what this platform commits to, is make you measurably better at the mathematics, the engineering and the finance that the industry actually tests for. That is the deal. Everything that follows, from arithmetic to order-book systems, exists to honour it.

blocks.title: Set your expectations now
blocks.md: This orientation module is deliberately light on formulas. The phases after it are not: expect real mathematics, real C++, and real finance, in that order of appearance. The time estimates on each lesson are honest, a 25-minute lesson means 25 minutes of genuine attention, and rushing the foundations shows up later.

guidedExercise.prompt: In your own words, write two or three sentences distinguishing finance in general from *quantitative* finance, and give one concrete example of a problem that specifically needs the quantitative approach.
hints: Ask yourself: what does the quantitative part add, what would you do differently with mathematics and software?
A good example names a decision and the computation behind it, e.g. quoting a price for an option.
guidedExercise.solution: **Model answer.** Finance in general is about allocating money and managing financial relationships, lending, investing, advising, transacting. Quantitative finance is the part of that where the decisions are produced by explicit mathematics, statistics and software: the answer is computed, not merely judged. A concrete example is option pricing: when a desk quotes a price for an option, it must translate market data and a model into a number within seconds, and quantify how much that number can move, a task that is impossible without quantitative machinery. By contrast, negotiating a client relationship or drafting a fund's marketing material is finance, but not particularly quantitative.

independentExercise.prompt: Write down which of the four problem areas, pricing, risk, trading, or investment, interests you most, one specific question inside it that you would like to be able to answer by the end of this platform, and one mathematical or computing skill that question seems to need. Keep your answer; we will refer back to it as you progress.
hints: Make the question specific enough that answering it is checkable, 'understand risk' is too vague, 'compute the maximum overnight loss on a two-position portfolio' is right.
Skill candidates: probability, statistics, C++ programming, linear algebra, numerical methods.
independentExercise.solution: **Model answer.** Area: risk. Question I want to answer: given a portfolio of two stocks with known positions, how much value could I lose on a bad day, and what assumptions does that estimate rest on? Skills it seems to need: probability and statistics (to model returns and tail behaviour), linear algebra (to handle many positions at once), and programming (to compute it on real data rather than by hand). This is exactly the kind of question the risk-management and statistics phases of the platform build toward.

commonMistakes: Treating 'quant finance' as a single job rather than a method used across pricing, risk, trading and investment.
Believing that learning a little Python is sufficient preparation, the mathematics and the software engineering are the substance.
Confusing platform promises with employment promises: preparation is measurable, hiring outcomes are not guaranteed by anyone honestly.
Skipping the orientation phase because it has no formulas, the context it builds makes later material far easier to place.
realWorldApplication: Every pricing quote, overnight risk report and execution algorithm in the industry is an instance of the same definition taught here: mathematics and software producing financial decisions. Knowing which of the four problem areas a piece of work belongs to tells you what skills it will exercise.
quantFinanceApplication: The four-area breakdown, pricing, risk, trading, investment, is how desks and funds actually organise work, and it maps directly onto the modules of this platform.
summary: Quantitative finance applies mathematics, statistics and computing to four problem areas: pricing, risk, trading and investment.
It is used across the industry, banks, asset managers, hedge funds, market makers, exchanges, vendors and regulators, by researchers, developers, traders and engineers.
The platform promises honest, measurable preparation: mathematics from zero, deep C++, real finance, checked by quizzes and assessments.
The platform does not promise employment; it promises capability, and capability is what you can control.

quiz.prompt: Which statement is the best definition of quantitative finance?
options: The application of mathematics, statistics and computing to pricing, risk, trading and investment problems
The use of trading software to buy and sell stocks quickly
Any finance work performed at a computer instead of on paper
The management of client relationships at investment banks
quiz.explanation: The definition covers the methods (maths, statistics, computing) and the four problem areas where they are applied. Option B describes only one narrow slice, and C and D confuse tooling or setting with substance.

quiz.prompt: Which of these tasks is most clearly quantitative finance?
options: Computing a portfolio's potential loss under a severe market scenario
Drafting the marketing brochure for a new fund
Choosing the colour scheme of a trading dashboard
quiz.explanation: Scenario-based loss computation is risk management, one of the four core problem areas. The other tasks are legitimate finance work but do not centre on mathematical modelling or computation.

quiz.prompt: Name the four problem areas of quantitative finance listed in this lesson.
quiz.modelAnswer: Pricing (valuation), risk (management), trading (and execution), and investment (portfolio management).
quiz.explanation: These four areas structure both the industry's work and this platform's curriculum.

quiz.prompt: Which of the following does this platform promise?
options: Honest, measurable preparation across mathematics, software engineering and finance
A guaranteed job offer upon completion
A specified minimum salary at any employer
quiz.explanation: The platform commits to honest content and measurable progress via quizzes, assessments and projects. Employment outcomes are explicitly not promised, any programme guaranteeing them would be dishonest.

quiz.prompt: A hedge fund, an asset manager and a market-making firm are mentioned in this lesson. Which pairing is correct?
options: Two Sigma, hedge fund; BlackRock, asset manager; Optiver, market maker
Two Sigma, asset manager; BlackRock, hedge fund; Optiver, bank
BlackRock, market maker; Optiver, hedge fund; Two Sigma, bank
quiz.explanation: Two Sigma is known as a data-driven hedge fund, BlackRock as one of the world's largest asset managers, and Optiver as a proprietary trading / market-making firm. Lesson 4 covers each institution type in detail.
